Placid

PLASS-id -- Latin placidus, 'gentle, quiet,' from placere, 'to please': the same root as please and pleasant. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Placid is not easily upset or excited.

Our placid old dog sleeps through thunderstorms and fireworks alike.

Worked Example

A toddler knocks a full glass of juice across the table, and the babysitter simply reaches for a towel, still smiling, without a single word of complaint.

Staying untroubled when most people would be rattled is exactly what placid describes. Unlike 'patient,' which is about waiting, placid is about not getting stirred up in the first place.

How Placid Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

calm

calm: free from disturbance

unflappable

unflappable: impossible to fluster, no matter what happens

untroubled

untroubled: showing no sign of worry

Antonyms

agitated

agitated: stirred up and restless

excitable

excitable: quick to get worked up

How Strong Is It? — calm → placid → unflappable

calm vs. placid

calm vs. placid: Calm is the plain, general word -- anyone can be calm for a moment, while placid describes a settled temperament that stays calm as a rule.

unflappable vs. placid

unflappable vs. placid: Unflappable is placid tested and proved: placid means not easily upset, while unflappable means nothing whatsoever can rattle you, even in an emergency.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — plac-

root — plac-: to please, to be gentle or calm (Latin (placere))

suffix — -id

suffix — -id: adjective-forming: tending to be (Latin (-idus))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin placidus meant 'gentle, quiet, pleasing,' from placere ('to please') -- a placid person is pleasant and untroubled, from the same root behind please, pleasant, and placate.

Use the root in a new word: placate

Use the root in a new word: placate: A free dessert did little to placate the furious customer.

Root Check

Word Choice

Placid describes people and animals with even temperaments, and also still water -- 'a placid lake.' Applied to a person it is usually a compliment, though it can hint that someone is a little too unbothered to react when they should.
